Technical Analysis: JPEG XS Compression Reduces 12G-SDI Latency by 30% in Live Production Environments

At the recent NAB Show, intoPIX announced the integration of JPEG XS compression into their IP-cores for live production environments, reducing latency by 30% compared to traditional uncompressed 12G-SDI transmission. This development is significant for broadcast CTOs and infrastructure engineers, as it directly impacts the real-time transport and signal integrity of live video feeds. The technology is based on the JPEG XS standard, which is designed for low-latency, low-complexity compression of video signals.

Operational ROI

The introduction of JPEG XS compression in live production environments can significantly reduce transmission costs and lower latency compared to traditional satellite or fibre transmission methods. By compressing video signals using JPEG XS, broadcast engineers can simplify signal routing and reduce the hardware rack footprint required for transmission, resulting in cost savings of up to 25% per year. This technology specifically affects the workflow step of signal transmission, where reduced latency and compressed signals enable more efficient and reliable live video feeds.

In comparison to the existing approach of using uncompressed 12G-SDI transmission, the JPEG XS compression method offers a more efficient and cost-effective solution. The reduced latency of 30% enables broadcast engineers to improve the overall quality of live video feeds, while the simplified signal routing and reduced hardware requirements result in lower operational costs. Additionally, the use of JPEG XS compression enables easier integration with other IP-based technologies, such as SMPTE ST 2110 and NMOS, which can further streamline live production workflows.

Security & Integration

The integration of JPEG XS compression into live production environments must be carefully considered in terms of security and integration with existing broadcast IT stacks. The JPEG XS standard is designed to be compliant with relevant industry standards, including SMPTE ST 2110 and NMOS, ensuring seamless integration with other IP-based technologies. From a cybersecurity perspective, the use of JPEG XS compression does not introduce any significant new risks, as the compressed signals are still transmitted over secure IP networks using protocols such as SRT or RIST. However, broadcast engineers must ensure that the IP-cores and software used for JPEG XS compression are properly configured and secured to prevent any potential vulnerabilities.

Engineering Takeaways

  • Deployment: The deployment of JPEG XS compression in live production environments requires a minimum network bandwidth of 10GbE and a hardware platform capable of supporting the intoPIX IP-cores, such as an FPGA or ASIC.
  • Compatibility: The JPEG XS compression technology is compliant with the SMPTE ST 2110-22 standard for transport of compressed video over IP networks, ensuring compatibility with other IP-based technologies and devices.
  • What to Watch: The upcoming update to the SMPTE ST 2110 standard, which is expected to include new specifications for JPEG XS compression, will be an important development for broadcast engineers to track, as it may introduce new features and requirements for the use of JPEG XS in live production environments.

The introduction of JPEG XS compression in live production environments signals a significant shift towards more efficient and cost-effective live video transmission methods. As a result, engineering teams should begin evaluating the integration of JPEG XS compression into their existing workflows and infrastructure, to take advantage of the reduced latency and operational costs offered by this technology.

Analysis: ST 2110 transport streams may be affected by AI-generated traffic, potentially altering bitrate and latency in streaming workflows, particularly when using AAC or Opus codecs for audio encoding. NMOS protocol may help manage such streams.
